title: Chinese Chess vs Modern Chess
summary: Collaboration (~53 min) with chess YouTuber Pietro (PietroCheckmate, on webcam): a Xiangqi-adapted army on an 8x8 chessboard versus a normal chess army, no clock. Chinese side: cannons (move like rooks, capture by jumping over exactly one screen piece at any distance), elephants (jump exactly two squares diagonally), soldiers/pawns (move and capture one step straight forward; after crossing the 5th rank also sideways), king (one step orthogonally only), horses (knight move but can't jump - blocked by an orthogonally adjacent piece), chariots (rooks), advisors (one step diagonal). Game 1 the narrator plays the Chinese army as White (early cannon g4->e4 mate threat); frames show a later game with sides swapped (Pietro with the Xiangqi army as White). Multiple games; Pietro lost the first 'horrifically'.
rules: 8x8 board; one side uses the Xiangqi-adapted army, the other a normal FIDE army; normal check/checkmate.
Cannon: moves like a rook without capturing; captures by jumping over exactly one piece (screen) along a rank/file and taking the first piece beyond it.
Elephant: moves exactly two squares diagonally (can't be blocked? Xiangqi blocks at the midpoint - not stated) [river restriction not applicable on 8x8].
Soldier (pawn): moves/captures one square straight forward; after crossing the 5th rank it may also move/capture one square sideways; no double step, no diagonal capture.
King (general): one step orthogonally only; palace confinement not confirmed.
Horse: knight move, but blocked if the orthogonally adjacent square in its direction is occupied (no jumping).
Chariot: rook. Advisor: one step diagonally (ferz).
